episodes.title: Broad River lynching (Spartanburg County, 1895)
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The Broad River lynching was the reported killing of an unnamed white woman and an unnamed Black man, whose bodies were found in and beside the Broad River in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, near the North Carolina line, in August 1895. A report described as "well-authenticated" attributed the deaths to a local band of White Caps punishing the pair for "miscegenation," though the newspaper headline called them only "Probably Lynched."

episodes.title: Lynching of two Black men at Camden, Arkansas (1895)
episodes.doubt: names, date and place from B-T:bt:3306/3307 (Jack and Jim Ware, hanged at Hampton, Calhoun Co., July 14, for the murder of a white man); our copies are one unnamed Camden-datelined brief; the Afro-American (1895-08-17, 'The Curse of Lynching') cites rewards for the hanging of two Black men in Calhoun County
episodes.summary: The lynching of two Black men at Camden, Arkansas, took place in or before late July 1895, when a mob overpowered the sheriff, took out two prisoners and hanged them. The men, who were not named, were said to have murdered a white man. The episode survives only as a one-sentence wire brief reprinted in small Northern Plains weeklies.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Harris
episodes.doubt: actor contested: a 200-man posse (Albany special) vs unknown men who took him from a bailiff (Moultrie letter)
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Harris took place on August 10, 1895, in western Colquitt County, Georgia, when a group of men killed Harris, an 18-year-old Black youth accused of assaulting an elderly white woman. Harris was captured near Camilla after a manhunt and shot to death on the way back to Colquitt County, though some reports said he had been burned or hanged. The story ran in papers across the country, often under headlines that approved the killing, and a Moultrie correspondent called it the county's first lynching.

episodes.title: Pursuit of the Fernandina jail escapees
episodes.doubt: deaths contested: the wire says all four drowned; a Florida weekly says no one was found and drowning 'hardly probable'
episodes.summary: The pursuit of the Fernandina jail escapees was a sheriffs' manhunt in late July 1895 near Fernandina, Florida, in which a posse fired on Black prisoners who had broken out of the Fernandina jail and drove them into the surf off Amelia beach. A widely reprinted wire dispatch reported that all four escapees, Tudor Brown, Willie Cook, Sam or Sim Echols and John Armstrong, drowned. A Florida weekly, however, reported that no one was found and judged drowning "hardly probable," so the coverage does not settle whether anyone died.

episodes.title: Lynching of Noah Anderson
episodes.summary: The lynching of Noah Anderson took place at New Richmond, Clermont County, Ohio, on the afternoon of August 21, 1895, when a crowd seized Anderson, a Black man, from the village marshal outside the jail and hanged him from a tree. He had been arrested hours earlier, accused of choking to death Franklin Friedman, an elderly bank president. Reports that Anderson was insane drew wide comment, especially in Southern papers.

episodes.title: Haile gold mine manhunt
episodes.summary: The Haile gold mine manhunt was the pursuit of Charles Lloyd, a Black mine worker, by a posse of white men in Lancaster County, South Carolina, in late August 1895, after he was accused of shooting two white youths, killing W. B. Welsh and wounding John Hough. The pursuers were said to be bent on lynching him, but he was captured, wounded, near Monroe, North Carolina, and jailed there. A widely reprinted wire story attributed to Lloyd a declaration that it was time for Black people to kill white men, a claim the local South Carolina reports did not repeat.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Delta County, Texas
episodes.doubt: the killing of William Stephens is g6 and Jeff Cole is a separate new event; Edora church burning (Lamar Co.) added separately
episodes.summary: The expulsion of Black residents from Delta County, Texas, was a campaign in the summer of 1895 in which notices posted by bands the press called "White Caps" ordered every Black resident of the county to leave or be hanged. Black families abandoned farms and standing crops, and a farmer named William Stephens, who stayed past his notice, was reported shot dead at his door, though a local merchant said he knew of no killing. The movement spread into neighboring Lamar County, where a Black church was burned, and the story ran in white papers across the country.

episodes.title: Killing of William Stephens
episodes.doubt: one Paris dispatch quotes a merchant near Glory who knew of no Black person shot by White Caps
episodes.summary: The killing of William Stephens was the shooting of a Black farmer at his door near Pacio, Delta County, Texas, in August 1895 by "white caps," after he stayed past a ten-day notice ordering him to leave. Carried from Paris, Texas, on his mother's word, the killing was reported within a white-cap campaign that had driven Black residents from Delta County "almost to a man." The wire story that spread the news also quoted a local merchant who knew of no such killing.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of the Atkins brothers
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of the Atkins brothers took place near Choctaw City and at Oklahoma City, Oklahoma Territory, at the end of July and beginning of August 1895, after "We" Atkins, a Black laborer, and one or two of his brothers were arrested and charged with the murder of Mrs. J. F. Mitchell. Crowds demanded the prisoner and made "numerous threats of lynching," and twenty-five deputies were reported guarding the men before "We" Atkins was moved to El Reno for safe keeping. White papers in Oklahoma, Kansas and beyond carried the case, most treating the accused's guilt as likely, while the fullest local account doubted the report that the woman had been sexually assaulted.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sam Sheeler
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Sam Sheeler took place at Otsego, Michigan, on August 19, 1895, when a crowd entered the jail, put a rope around the neck of Sheeler, a Black man accused of robbing and attempting to assault a woman, and dragged him from his cell. With the noose drawn tight he confessed and named companions, after which he was spared and returned to jail while posses hunted the other men. The story ran by wire across the country, and Virginia papers singled it out as a lynching attempt in the "staid law abiding North."

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Haggard
episodes.summary: The lynching of Bob Haggard was the hanging of a Black man by a mob in Kentucky in mid-July 1895, after he was accused of assaulting a young woman named Miss Elkin. Within days a wire report datelined Ford, Ky., said he had been innocent and that the story of the crime was false, and newspapers across the country ran the item under headlines such as "Lynched an Innocent Man." Kentucky papers placed the lynching at Winchester, and no report of an arrest was found.

episodes.title: Walterboro jail lynching threat (1895)
episodes.summary: The Walterboro jail lynching threat was an August 1895 episode in South Carolina in which a mob from Hampton county was reported preparing to lynch six Black prisoners held in the Colleton county jail at Walterboro. Deputies spirited the men out of town through the swamps and by boat and train to the state penitentiary in Columbia, and no one was harmed. South Carolina and Savannah papers told the story as a narrow escape, under headlines such as "Defeated Lynchers" and "Ropes for Six."

episodes.title: Brookside riot (1895)
episodes.doubt: wire reports 3-4 Black dead and Deputy Baxter dead; the local paper discredits the bodies and has Baxter alive; victim list mixes deputies (Wood, Baxter) and duplicate names
episodes.summary: The Brookside riot was an armed clash on the night of July 30, 1895, at a Sloss Iron and Steel Company mining camp west of Birmingham, Alabama, in which white miners fought and pursued Black miners after Deputy Sheriff A. T. Wood was shot dead making an arrest. Wire reports said three or four Black men were killed and that white miners had captives beneath a noose when Sheriff Morrow forced their surrender, though the local Birmingham Age-Herald discredited the reports of bodies. Papers nationwide carried it as a "race riot," and the rescue drew editorial comment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Bennett
episodes.summary: The lynching of Robert Bennett was the killing of a young Black preacher on July 4, 1895, after a mob took him from the pulpit of a church at Hope Henry, five miles west of Lake City, Florida. He was accused of an assault on a white girl or woman, an accusation the reports give in differing forms. In August several white men were charged with the lynching and discharged at a preliminary trial, and the case drew an indignation meeting at Lake City and comment in the Black press.

episodes.title: Lynching of Squire Loftin
episodes.summary: The lynching of Squire Loftin took place near Lexington, Lee County, Texas, in late July 1895, when a mob took Loftin, described as a Black man, from custody and hanged him from a tree. He had been accused of attempting to assault a 12-year-old girl, and the papers reported that he had also confessed to a murder committed seven years earlier. The Shiner Gazette in Texas reported it in some detail, while papers across the Midwest carried it as a brief wire or digest item.

episodes.title: Lynching of a farm hand in Simpson County, Mississippi (1895)
episodes.summary: The lynching of a farm hand in Simpson County, Mississippi, took place in late August 1895, when a crowd of local men hanged an unnamed Black farm hand, about 21 years old, from a tree in the Strong River swamp near Westville. He was accused of fathering a child born to the 14-year-old daughter of a local farmer, John Mulligan. Dispatches from Jackson ran in at least thirteen white newspapers across the country, some of them treating the case as unusual or questioning the father's conduct, while no Black newspaper account has been found.

episodes.title: Killing of James Mason
episodes.summary: The killing of James Mason was the shooting of a Black man by a band of seven men at Dangerfield, Texas, on the night of August 1, 1895. The men called Mason out of his house and shot him dead, then fired into the house, wounding his wife, who was not expected to live, and one of his children. Papers outside Texas carried the news as a short wire item, one under the headline "Seven Texas Lynchers" and weekly digests attributing it to "whitecaps".

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Jones
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Jones took place about 1:30 a.m. on August 22, 1895, when a band of about twenty-five masked men broke into the Drew County jail at Monticello, Arkansas, took out Jones, a Black prisoner, and hanged him from a tree at the edge of town. Jones was accused of killing a white man named Beltzhoover near Tillar and had shot a member of a pursuing party during a jail break five days earlier. The story ran nationally by wire, and the local weekly condemned the mob while calling Jones a confessed murderer.

episodes.title: Lynching of Emmett Divers
episodes.summary: The lynching of Emmett Divers took place early on August 15, 1895, when masked men took Divers, a Black man accused of the rape and murder of Mrs. J. W. Cain, from two deputies and hanged him from a bridge east of Fulton, Callaway County, Missouri. His body was then paraded in Fulton, shot at, and hung from a telegraph pole at the request of the dead woman's husband. The case ran on the national wire and drew editorial argument in Missouri and in two Black weeklies in Kansas.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of Black log cutters at Thornton, Arkansas
episodes.summary: The whitecapping of Black log cutters at Thornton, Arkansas, was a warning delivered in the summer of 1895 by men described as 'whitecappers' to the Black employees of mill owner W. R. Pearson in Calhoun County, telling them they would no longer be allowed to cut logs. The notice halted Pearson's logging until he could find other labor, and Pearson attributed it to a determination to keep Black men from competing in mill work. The episode survives in a single Camden dispatch that ran in Arkansas state-news columns in early August.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Mitchell and Mike Stevens
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of George Mitchell and Mike Stevens was an attempt by a mob, in late July 1895, to storm the jail at Live Oak, Florida, and lynch two Black men condemned for the murder of a white man, Alfred Ryberg. The attempt failed, and both men were later hanged by the state, Mitchell on August 1 and Stevens on September 18. Papers reported the mob attack in a single sentence of a dispatch that cast lynching as the expected alternative to clemency.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charlie Burwell
episodes.doubt: later reports say the Farmer assailants killed him to keep him from betraying them (B-T: 'to prevent reporting on the murderers')
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charlie Burwell was the hanging of an elderly Black man near Meridian, Mississippi, on a Saturday night in late July 1895. Early reports said he was killed on suspicion of a July 4 assault on a storekeeping couple, but later accounts said the real assailants killed him because he had been promised a reward to find them. The story ran as a wire dispatch or one-line brief in papers across the country and in Mississippi state columns.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Henry Harris
episodes.doubt: threat undated (after the alleged crime of early July); the only death is his legal execution on 1895-08-23
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of James Henry Harris took place in King and Queen County, Virginia, in the summer of 1895, when a mob threatened a young Black man charged with attempting to assault a six-year-old white girl as he was being taken to jail. The arresting officer, the child's father, turned the would-be lynchers away, and Harris was hanged under a court sentence at King and Queen Courthouse on 23 August 1895. White papers treated the officer's protection of the prisoner as remarkable and praised it in news stories and an editorial.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Johnson
episodes.summary: The lynching of Tom Johnson was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Hattiesburg, Mississippi, on Friday, July 26, 1895. Accused of an ax and pistol attack on the Hartfield family, he was taken from jail, escaped, was recaptured and was shot to death before a large crowd after a reported confession. Mississippi papers praised the killing, digests elsewhere turned it into a burning, and the New-York Tribune ridiculed it.

episodes.title: Raids on Black churches in Lafayette and Taylor counties, Florida
episodes.summary: The raids on Black churches in Lafayette and Taylor counties, Florida, were attacks by armed white men on church services in July 1895, reported by Rev. W. Gillisle, presiding elder of the Live Oak district of the African Methodist church. Gillisle said crowds broke up his services in both counties and drove him out, and that churches were being raided, congregations dispersed and pastors driven away. No one was reported shot, but the story ran under the headline "A Reign of Terror" as far away as Idaho, Minnesota and Michigan.

episodes.title: Whipping of Cyrus Davis
episodes.summary: The whipping of Cyrus Davis was a whitecapping attack on a Black barber of Blackville, Barnwell County, South Carolina, who was carried into the country and flogged on the night of August 8, 1895. Davis survived, and he said he had been told the beating was punishment for his testimony as a witness in a murder case. Papers in South Carolina called it an outrage, while New York papers reported it as part of a wave of whitecapping in the county.

episodes.title: Whitecapping on the Nevins farm, Barnwell County
episodes.summary: The whitecapping on the Nevins farm was an attack by white men described as "white caps" on Black people living on the farm of H. H. Nevins in Barnwell County, South Carolina, in the summer of 1895. At least one Black man was whipped, and Nevins told the governor that all his hands had been driven from his place. The case drew attention because it reached Governor Evans during a wider run of whitecapping complaints from the county.

episodes.title: Shooting of William Brown by Constable Cozzens
episodes.summary: The shooting of William Brown was an incident in Carlin, Nevada, in mid-1895, in which Constable Cozzens shot Brown, whom the local paper described as "the colored man." Brown survived, was indicted for burglary, pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to two years in the penitentiary in early August 1895. The shooting is known only from a single sentence in an Elko newspaper's local column.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Harriman, Tennessee
episodes.doubt: the arrest of nearly fifty Black men on suspicion is part of the episode
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching at Harriman, Tennessee, was an August 1895 manhunt in which armed searching parties and police bloodhounds pursued a Black man accused of assaulting a young white girl, while newspapers reported he would be lynched if caught. A man arrested in Atlanta, named in most reports as George Gaither, was returned amid rumors of a posse and released when the girl failed to identify him. Nearly fifty Black men were arrested on suspicion; no lynching was reported.

episodes.title: Killing of Jerry Johnson
episodes.summary: The killing of Jerry Johnson took place near Farmington, Tennessee, where the bullet-riddled body of Johnson, a Black man, was found on August 27, 1895. He had been warned days earlier to leave over an alleged improper proposal to a young girl, and wire reports said he was supposed to have been killed by a mob. Northern and western weeklies later reduced the story to a one-line item stating that he had been lynched for an insulting proposal to a white girl.

episodes.title: Whipping of Mat Wilson and Lou Clemmons
episodes.summary: The whipping of Mat Wilson and Lou Clemmons was a night flogging of two women by "a party of lynchers" at Liberty, Casey County, Kentucky, on a Tuesday night, apparently July 30, 1895. The next day the county sheriff jailed the two women at Stanford, and the only report of the whipping, a local correspondence, used it to argue for stricter enforcement of the law rather than lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Stroman
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Stroman was the killing of a Black man by a citizen posse near Wharton, Texas, in August 1895, after he was accused of shooting Deputy Sheriff Frank Brown. The posse that held him reported that he had "escaped," but a later Wharton dispatch said he had been lynched below town and buried. The same dispatch said the "unwritten law" had been invoked and that there was very little comment.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Wesley
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of John Wesley took place in St. Louis County, Missouri, in late August and early September 1895, when armed citizens' posses hunted Wesley, a Black man accused of attempting to assault an aged widow at Manchester, intending to hang him. Deputy sheriffs captured him early on September 4 and lodged him in the county jail at Clayton, where the last reports leave him. Wire dispatches carried the manhunt nationally, often under headlines forecasting a hanging.

episodes.title: Whipping of Bill Criswell
episodes.summary: The whipping of Bill Criswell was a mob assault in August 1895 in which residents of Guthrie, Missouri, caught Criswell, a Black man, and beat him with buggy whips. According to the only report found, he had paraded the village streets with a gun to protest how his friend Emmett Divers had been "disposed of". The Mexico Weekly Ledger reported the beating as a deserved lesson.

episodes.title: Killing of Frank Maxwell
episodes.summary: The killing of Frank Maxwell took place in Augusta, Georgia, about daylight on August 27, 1895, when two city policemen chased and shot Maxwell, a Black convict who had escaped from the county gang. Maxwell died within minutes, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide the same day. The case drew only brief notice in the white press of Georgia and South Carolina.

episodes.title: Greenville lynching of July 1895
episodes.doubt: our sources (a sermon and a church paper) name no victim; identified with B-T:bt:3308 Ira Johnson, Greenville SC, Monday 1895-07-15
episodes.summary: The Greenville lynching of July 1895 was a killing in Greenville, apparently in South Carolina, that took place on a Monday morning shortly before July 23, 1895, and that a church paper's correspondent called "the recent lynching in Greenville." The surviving coverage names no victim, accusation or perpetrators. It is known only from a pastor's sermon and a Methodist paper's editorial and letters, which condemned lynching.

episodes.title: Killing of James Burns
episodes.summary: The killing of James Burns took place on the outskirts of Sylvania, Georgia, in early August 1895, when a Black man accused of an earlier murder was shot and beaten to death by white men trying to arrest him. According to the Savannah Morning News, Burns was hit seven times and finally knocked down with a rifle after an exchange of sixteen shots with his pursuers, neither of whom was hurt. A wire version carried by papers from Virginia to South Dakota told the story as "a sensational battle between officers and a desperate criminal" in which Burns took eleven bullets.

episodes.title: Killing of Andy Hightower
episodes.summary: The killing of Andy Hightower was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a deputy sheriff and a second man at Rome, Georgia, on the afternoon of August 3, 1895. Hightower, said to be wanted on warrants elsewhere, died the next morning after physicians had expected him to recover, and a coroner's jury was convened.

episodes.title: Smyrna riot (1895)
episodes.doubt: Berry Smith reported wounded and missing, fate unknown; who fired first disputed; Jesse Hardeman, the hunted man, was not found
episodes.summary: The Smyrna riot was an armed clash near midnight on 1 August 1895 near Smyrna, Cobb County, Georgia, in which a white posse hunting Jesse Hardeman, a Black farm hand accused of attempting to assault a white woman, stopped and fired on his father, his brother and two other Black men. Three of the Black men were shot, a fourth was missing afterward, and a white man, Charley Dowda, was wounded in the hand. Wire reports called it a "pitched battle" and warned of a Black "uprising"; sworn testimony split over who fired first.

episodes.title: Excelsior Springs jail whipping
episodes.summary: The Excelsior Springs jail whipping took place on the night of August 27, 1895, when men took two prisoners, one Black and one white, from the city jail at Excelsior Springs, Missouri, and whipped them. Both men were then released, and wire reports headlined the attack as the work of "whitecaps" and said the town's Black residents were pressing for a legal investigation.

episodes.title: Aberdeen constable shooting (1895)
episodes.doubt: 'Butler' county came from a party ticket on the page; a Maysville paper's Aberdeen may be Aberdeen, Ohio
episodes.summary: The Aberdeen constable shooting was the pursuit of an unnamed Black man at Aberdeen on the morning of 24 August 1895, during which Constable Dawson fired several shots at him. The man, said to have shot a man at Lewisburg some time earlier, escaped, and the incident is known only from a single brief item in a Maysville, Kentucky, daily.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Stockton
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of James Stockton took place near Broad Ripple, Indiana, in August 1895, when an armed mob chased and captured Stockton, a Black man accused of firing at a farmer's grandson. According to a wire report, older citizens kept the crowd from lynching him only with difficulty; he was arrested and charged with the shooting.

episodes.title: Ducking of a Black woman at Edinburg, Virginia
episodes.summary: The ducking of a Black woman at Edinburg, Virginia, was an assault in the summer of 1895 in which a woman from Woodstock was ducked in Stony Creek and ordered to leave the town within three days. She left, and the only known report, a paragraph in the Edinburg column of the Woodstock Shenandoah Herald, approved of the outcome.

episodes.title: Racine street laborers' fight (1895)
episodes.summary: The Racine street laborers' fight was a brawl on August 9, 1895, in Racine, Wisconsin, in which a discharged white laborer attacked the Black foreman of a city street crew and white men and Black laborers then fought on a principal street. Police ended the fight, and the foreman, Lockhardt, was the only man reported arrested. Wisconsin papers printed the story under the headline "Race War at Racine."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Solomon Marable, Pokey Barnes and Mary Abernathy
episodes.doubt: threat reported in press dispatches, denied by residents
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Solomon Marable, Pokey Barnes and Mary Abernathy was a reported threat of mob violence against three Black prisoners charged with the murder of Lucy Jane Pollard in Lunenburg County, Virginia, in June and July 1895. The prisoners were tried at Lunenburg Courthouse under the guard of three militia companies and sentenced to hang; none was harmed by a crowd. In August, Richmond critics called the convictions verdicts dictated by a mob, and Lunenburg citizens answered that the danger had been invented.

episodes.title: Police shooting at Andrew Mills
episodes.summary: The police shooting at Andrew Mills took place in Birmingham, Alabama, at about 11 p.m. on 1 August 1895, when two police officers chased Mills, a Black man described as an escaped convict, and fired four shots at him. None of the shots was reported to have hit him, and he escaped; one officer hurt his knee in a fall during the chase.

episodes.title: Shooting of Sol Russell
episodes.summary: The shooting of Sol Russell took place on a Saturday in August 1895 in Brick Store district near Covington, Georgia, when Frank Patrick wounded Russell, a Black man, while Patrick and several other men were trying to arrest him. Russell was hit in the face and eyes with bird shot and was jailed in Covington, where doctors thought he might lose an eye.

episodes.title: Killing of Ovide Belizaire
episodes.summary: The killing of Ovide Belizaire was the fatal shooting of a Black man in his own house in Louisiana, by a band of masked, armed men, at night shortly before 3 August 1895. A coroner's inquest placed the guilt on no one, and the Lafayette Gazette, in an editorial reprinted by the Abbeville Meridional, condemned the killing as an unprovoked murder.

episodes.title: Spring Valley race riot of 1895
episodes.doubt: injuries and missing contested (14 named injured in the wire, 1-3 locally); victim list has OCR variants of the same people
episodes.summary: The Spring Valley race riot of 1895 was an attack on Sunday, August 4, 1895, by a mob of several hundred miners on "The Location," a Black miners' settlement near the No. 3 shaft at Spring Valley, Illinois, that drove its residents from their homes. Wire reports named fourteen Black men, women and children who were shot, clubbed or trampled, and the next day a mass meeting of miners ordered the remaining Black residents out of town. Local and outside accounts disputed how many were hurt or killed, and the expelled miners returned to work under guard on August 9.

episodes.title: Winston jail riot
episodes.doubt: at least one of the Black crowd died of militia gunfire; 'another' implies an earlier death; Tuttle himself unharmed
episodes.summary: The Winston jail riot took place on the night of August 11, 1895, in Winston, North Carolina, when an armed crowd of Black residents gathered at the jail to protect a Black prisoner, Arthur Tuttle, from a rumored lynching and was scattered by volleys from the militia and deputies. Several of the crowd were wounded and at least one later died; about fifty Black men were jailed and prosecuted, and hundreds left the town. The dispatch ran nationally, often under the heading "race war".

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Mitchell Smith
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Henry Mitchell Smith took place in Lexington, Kentucky, in August 1895, when a Black man jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman near Payne Station was threatened by a crowd at the Fayette County jail. Wire dispatches carried in papers from Rhode Island to Utah predicted that he would be lynched, but county and circuit judges posted armed guards, no attack on the jail was reported, and Smith was sentenced in September to hang.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Matthew Lewis and Jesse Ray
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Matthew Lewis and Jesse Ray was an assault by a mob of about forty men on the jail at Springfield, Washington County, Kentucky, early on Sunday, August 11, 1895. The mob got the jail keys but could not open the cells, fired into them without hitting anyone, and left; the sheriff then moved both men to Louisville. Papers across the country ran the story because the would-be lynchers were said to have been too drunk to unlock the doors.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Rufus Buck gang
episodes.doubt: first wire called them 'Creek negroes'; later reports: Uchee/Creek Indians except Lucky Davis, described as 'a negro'
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of the Rufus Buck gang took place in the Creek Nation, Indian Territory, in August 1895, when crowds of citizens at Okmulgee and Muskogee tried to take five captured men from the officers holding them in order to lynch them. The officers slipped away from both crowds and took the prisoners by train to the federal jail at Fort Smith, Arkansas, where a court later sentenced them to hang.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Jim Cullins
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Jim Cullins took place on the night of 24 August 1895 in Lynchburg, Virginia, when Police Officer J. R. Coomes shot Cullins, a Black man, during an attempted arrest. Two of four shots struck Cullins, who was reported "probably fatally wounded," though no later report of his death or recovery was found.

episodes.title: Mob pursuit of Henry Williams in Cincinnati
episodes.summary: The mob pursuit of Henry Williams took place in Cincinnati, Ohio, on August 12, 1895, when a crowd chased Williams, a Black man, through the streets after his companion Thomas Jones was accused of stabbing a white man. The crowd, put at 300 in the chase and about 2,000 at the depot, knocked Williams down before police held it back by drawing their pistols. The story ran as a short wire item in papers from Texas to Minnesota, one of which headlined it as a rescue by the police.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Wade
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Henry Wade was a failed attempt in August 1895 to lynch a Black man held for the shooting death of Henry Hightower, a young white man, at Martindale, Texas. Wade escaped by running to officers for protection and was afterwards held in jail at Seguin. The episode was reported in two short dispatches from Luling in the Fort Worth Gazette.

episodes.title: Killing of Berry's brother at Tippecanoe, Ohio
episodes.summary: The killing of Berry's brother at Tippecanoe, Ohio, was the fatal shooting of an unnamed Black man by the marshal of New Philadelphia in mid-August 1895, during an attempt to arrest his brother, a "colored man" named Berry. The marshal was wounded in the wrist and Berry escaped, and the episode reached readers outside Ohio only as a brief wire item.

episodes.title: Killing of Eli Williams
episodes.doubt: attacker unknown; found by the lone-actor re-check of Aug 1895
episodes.summary: The killing of Eli Williams was the fatal shooting of a Black preacher in his pulpit during Sunday services at a church near Mitchell Station, Alabama, on July 28, 1895. The gunman, believed to have fired from outside the building, was never identified in the coverage, and two Black men standing outside were held only as witnesses. The story circulated nationally as a short wire item under headlines such as "Assassinated in the Pulpit."

episodes.title: Killing of Ernest Green
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; found by the lone-actor re-check of Aug 1895
episodes.summary: The killing of Ernest Green was the fatal shooting of a Black boy, 13 or 14 years old, by Elizabeth M. Flagler, daughter of the army's chief of ordnance, who fired from an upstairs window at boys taking pears outside her family's home in Washington, D.C., on August 2, 1895. A coroner's jury found that same evening that she had fired "carelessly and indifferently" but could not be held, a verdict that drew protest from Black Washingtonians and comment across the country. She later gave $10,000 bail to await a grand jury, which had not taken up the case by the end of September.

episodes.title: Killing of William Williams
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; found by the lone-actor re-check of Aug 1895
episodes.summary: The killing of William Williams was the fatal shooting of an elderly Black farmhand by J. Z. Dodson, the white overseer of C. M. Cunningham's plantation on the Ogeechee River near Burroughs station, Georgia, on August 10, 1895. A coroner's jury ruled it accidental, but Williams's brother charged that Dodson had tried to kill him before, and Black residents threatened Dodson.
